patient.name: Brian Fitzgerald
patient.complaint: Collapsed while walking up a hill to church; chest tightness on exertion for 3 months
background: Retired bus driver from Croydon, lives with his wife
GP heard 'a murmur' 4 years ago; never followed up
Takes ramipril and metformin; no allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely valve abnormality?' from a murmur description: ejection systolic at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis; early diastolic at the left sternal edge with a collapsing pulse is aortic regurgitation.

points: Brian, 82, **collapsed** walking uphill; awake within a minute.
Three months of **chest tightness** on exertion, eased by rest.
Breathless after one flight of stairs.
No palpitations before the collapse; no tongue biting.

steps.lead: Brian's valve between the **LV and aorta** has narrowed: **aortic stenosis**, which obstructs LV outflow.
At 82, Brian's stenosis is almost certainly **degenerative calcification**. A younger patient would make you think **bicuspid** valve.

points: Pulse: **slow-rising**, small volume; BP 112/90 (narrow pulse pressure).
Systolic **thrill** at the right upper sternal edge.
Harsh **ejection systolic murmur**, 2nd right ICS, radiating to **both carotids**.
Fine crackles at both lung bases.

steps.lead: Brian has the **triad** (angina, syncope, exertional dyspnoea) and the classic signs: **ESM** to the carotids and **pulsus parvus et tardus**.

steps.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis for Brian?
steps.r: ESM radiating to the carotids, slow-rising pulse, soft S2 and exertional syncope is **aortic stenosis**. Sclerosis does not radiate and has a normal S2 and pulse.

steps.lead: Brian's **soft S2** and **S4** point to **severe** AS. The eponymous signs in this subsection belong to **aortic regurgitation**, his main differential.

steps.title: Aortic stenosis vs aortic regurgitation
head: Feature
Aortic stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
rows: **Ejection systolic**, right upper sternal edge, to carotids

steps.lead: Brian's murmur **radiates to the carotids**, his S2 is soft and his pulse is slow-rising: this is not **aortic sclerosis**.
Brian's problem is chronic. A sudden severe **acute AR**, most often from **aortic dissection**, would present with shock and acute heart failure.

steps.text: Exertional syncope in an elderly patient with an ESM is **aortic stenosis** until proven otherwise. Do not label it a simple faint or 'mechanical fall'.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (transthoracic echocardiogram) or 'Which is the most likely ECG finding?' (left ventricular hypertrophy).

steps.lead: Brian's first tests in ED are an **ECG** (looking for LVH) and a **chest X-ray** (cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema).

visual.title: Brian's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus rhythm. Tall R waves in V5-V6 and deep S in V1-V2 meet voltage criteria; lateral T inversion is the LVH 'strain' pattern.

steps.q: Which test confirms Brian's diagnosis and grades its severity?
steps.r: **Transthoracic echo** is the gold standard: it shows the valve, the pressure gradient, the valve area and LV function.

steps.lead: Brian's **TTE** shows a heavily calcified tricuspid valve with a high **pressure gradient** across it.

steps.title: Brian's echo and bloods
steps.text: Every marker says **severe** AS, and the LV is starting to fail.

visual.title: Peak transvalvular gradient
visual.label: Brian 72 mmHg
visual.caption: A gradient above 40 mmHg, or symptoms, means referral for valve replacement.

steps.lead: Brian meets several **AVR referral criteria**: Vmax over 5 m/s, LVEF under 55% and BNP over twice normal. His aortic root is normal, so no root surveillance.

steps.text: The ECG in AS shows **LVH**; the echo **confirms** the diagnosis. If the question asks for the **diagnostic** test, the answer is the **echo**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where severe or symptomatic AS means valve replacement, and the patient's age and fitness choose mechanical, bioprosthetic or TAVI.

steps.lead: Brian's **syncope** with severe AS is a **red flag**: he is admitted and referred urgently, not sent home.
Brian's basal crackles respond to **furosemide** for symptom relief. Monitoring alone would only suit **mild, asymptomatic** AS.

steps.q: Brian is 82, diabetic and frail, with severe symptomatic AS. Which intervention?
steps.r: **TAVI** suits less fit, higher-risk patients, typically over 80. Medical therapy alone does not change prognosis in severe symptomatic AS.

visual.title: Which valve? Age guide
visual.label: Brian 82
visual.caption: Age, life expectancy, fitness for surgery and anticoagulation risk decide the valve.

steps.lead: Brian's gradient is **above 40 mmHg** and he is symptomatic, so he is referred for replacement. At 82 and frail, the heart team choose **TAVI**.
After TAVI, Brian's **heart failure** and any **arrhythmias** are treated as they arise. A mechanical valve would have meant lifelong **warfarin**.
Brian's referral used the **severity criteria** (Vmax, valve area, LVEF, BNP). The INR target applies only to mechanical valves.

steps.text: Mechanical valves need **warfarin**, not a DOAC. DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical heart valves.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why AS causes LVH and a slow-rising pulse, why AR gives a wide pulse pressure, or what causes the Austin Flint murmur.

steps.lead: Brian's LV has pumped against a **fixed obstruction** for years, thickening concentrically; now it is starting to fail.

steps.title: From calcified valve to heart failure
nodes: Stiff LV, raised filling pressure; supply-demand mismatch → angina

steps.lead: Blood is forced slowly through Brian's narrow, stiff valve: a **slow-rising pulse**, and the immobile leaflets barely make a sound as they close (**soft S2**).

steps.q: Why does aortic regurgitation cause a wide pulse pressure?
o: High diastolic pressure from LV stiffness
Low diastolic pressure from rapid runoff back into the LV
Low systolic pressure from outflow obstruction
steps.r: Blood runs back into the LV in diastole, so **diastolic pressure falls**; the large stroke volume raises systolic pressure.

steps.lead: Unlike Brian's thick, small LV, a patient with AR has a **dilated** LV (eccentric hypertrophy) and a **wide pulse pressure** from diastolic runoff.
In AR, the regurgitant jet hits the anterior mitral leaflet, stopping it opening fully: a functional **mitral stenosis** murmur, the **Austin Flint**.
Brian's valve calcified in his 80s. A **bicuspid** valve calcifies decades earlier because of **turbulent flow** over abnormal leaflets.

visual.title: Peak gradient: tricuspid vs bicuspid valve
visual.caption: Bicuspid valves reach severe stenosis decades earlier; degenerative AS appears in the 70s-80s.

mcq.q: What is the classic triad of symptomatic aortic stenosis?
What is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in the UK?
Which murmur is heard in aortic regurgitation?
o: Early diastolic at the left sternal edge
Ejection systolic at the right upper sternal edge
mcq.r: **Early diastolic**, high-pitched, blowing, at the **left sternal edge**.

mcq.q: Which sign distinguishes aortic sclerosis from aortic stenosis?
o: Murmur does not radiate to the carotids
Murmur loudest at the right upper sternal edge
mcq.r: Sclerosis: **no carotid radiation**, normal S2 and normal pulse.

mcq.q: Head nodding with each heartbeat in aortic regurgitation is called?
mcq.r: **De Musset's**. Quincke's is nail bed, Muller's is uvula, Corrigan's is carotid.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for aortic valve disease?
Which ECG finding is typical of aortic stenosis?
Which peak gradient threshold prompts referral for valve replacement?
What is the target INR for a mechanical aortic valve (per the notes)?
Which type of LV hypertrophy develops in aortic stenosis?
mcq.r: **Concentric** LVH from pressure overload; AR gives eccentric (volume overload).

technique.stem: A 79 year old woman has had breathlessness on exertion for 6 months and fainted twice while gardening. Her pulse is 70 bpm and slow-rising, and her BP is 118/94 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur loudest in the 2nd right intercostal space, radiating to the carotids. The second heart sound is quiet.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A murmur diagnosis: time it, place it, check radiation.
Exertional syncope, slow-rising pulse, **narrow pulse pressure**, ESM to carotids, soft S2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Severe aortic stenosis.**

elim: AR is early diastolic with a collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure.
Sclerosis does not radiate to the carotids; S2 and pulse are normal.
HCM is younger, murmur at the left sternal edge, louder on Valsalva, no carotid radiation.
MR is pansystolic at the apex radiating to the axilla.

steps.x: **C. Aortic stenosis.** ESM to carotids + soft S2 + slow-rising pulse.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids found at a routine check. He has mild exertional breathlessness. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/86 mmHg. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' investigation: the test that confirms and grades the lesion.

clues: ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
steps.x: Suspected AS with symptoms and LVH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transthoracic echo**: valve structure and gradient.

elim: MRI is a later adjunct, not the gold standard.
CXR may show cardiomegaly but cannot grade the valve.
Angiography assesses coronaries before surgery, not the valve diagnosis.
Exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiogram.** Gold standard for valve disease.

technique.stem: A 54 year old man has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis due to a bicuspid aortic valve. He is otherwise fit, works full time and has no bleeding history. He wants a valve that will last as long as possible.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management: choose the valve type for this patient.
Young, fit, can take warfarin, wants durability.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mechanical valve**, lifelong warfarin (target INR 3.0).

elim: Valvuloplasty is a temporary bridge in adults.
Bioprosthetic valves wear out; better for older patients.
Symptomatic severe AS needs replacement, not monitoring.
TAVI is for frail, high-risk patients, typically over 80.

steps.x: **D. Mechanical valve with warfarin.** Young and fit = mechanical.

technique.stem: A 60 year old man has severe aortic regurgitation. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal mitral valve.
technique.q: Which is the most likely cause of the apical murmur?
o: Regurgitant jet impairing mitral valve opening

steps.x: Mechanism of a second murmur.

clues: rumbling mid-diastolic murmur at the apex
steps.x: A mitral stenosis-like murmur with a **normal** mitral valve: **Austin Flint**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The AR jet hits the anterior mitral leaflet and **stops it opening fully**.

elim: Echo shows a normal mitral valve.
A myxoma would be seen on echo.
Prolapse gives a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur.
A VSD is pansystolic at the left sternal edge.

steps.x: **D. Regurgitant jet impairing mitral opening.** Austin Flint = functional MS.

practice.stem: An 80 year old man has chest tightness when walking his dog and has had two episodes of light-headedness on exertion. His pulse rate is 68 bpm, slow-rising, and BP 116/92 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids.
practice.q: Which is the most likely valve abnormality?
practice.e: Angina and presyncope on exertion with a slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure and an ESM radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis.

steps.x: Which valve: time and place the murmur.
Triad features with the classic murmur and pulse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aortic stenosis.**

elim: AR is diastolic with a collapsing pulse.
MR is pansystolic to the axilla.
MS is mid-diastolic at the apex, often with AF.
TR is pansystolic at the left lower sternal edge with giant v waves.

steps.x: **B. Aortic stenosis.** ESM to carotids + exertional symptoms.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man who grew up in Nigeria has had increasing breathlessness and fatigue for a year. He had rheumatic fever as a child. His pulse is 84 bpm and collapsing, and his BP is 158/42 mmHg. There is a high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, loudest leaning forward in expiration.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure and early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge after rheumatic fever is aortic regurgitation.

steps.x: A murmur diagnosis.

clues: had rheumatic fever as a child
early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
steps.x: Rheumatic history, **wide pulse pressure**, collapsing pulse, **EDM**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aortic regurgitation** (rheumatic).

elim: AS is systolic with a narrow pulse pressure.
MS is a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex.
PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur.
Pulmonary regurgitation does not cause a collapsing pulse.

steps.x: **A. Aortic regurgitation.** EDM + collapsing pulse + wide pulse pressure.

practice.stem: A 46 year old man has exertional chest pain and breathlessness. He has no cardiovascular risk factors. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/96 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, preceded by an ejection click. Echocardiography shows a severely stenosed aortic valve with two leaflets.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his aortic stenosis?
practice.e: Severe AS in a middle-aged patient with two leaflets and an ejection click is a bicuspid valve. Degenerative calcification presents in the elderly.

steps.x: Cause of AS: the age decides.
Young for AS, a click, **two leaflets**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bicuspid aortic valve.**

elim: Degenerative AS is typically over 70.
Endocarditis causes regurgitation, with fever.
Marfan's causes root dilation and AR.
Rheumatic AS usually coexists with mitral disease.

steps.x: **A. Bicuspid aortic valve.** Younger AS = bicuspid.

practice.stem: An 84 year old woman has exertional breathlessness. Echocardiography shows severe aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 78 mmHg. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 110/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Severe AS gives a slow-rising, small-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) and a soft S2. A collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure are AR.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question in severe AS.
Severe AS with a **narrow pulse pressure**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Slow-rising pulse**, soft S2.

elim: Collapsing pulse is AR.
S2 is soft or absent in severe AS.
Apical pansystolic is MR.
Pulse pressure is narrow in AS.

steps.x: **D. Slow-rising pulse.** Pulsus parvus et tardus.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has a 2 year history of breathlessness. He has a collapsing pulse, his BP is 164/48 mmHg and pulse rate 88 bpm, and there is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His nail beds visibly pulsate when gentle pressure is applied to the tip of a fingernail.
practice.q: Which is the name of the nail bed sign?
practice.e: Visible capillary pulsation in the nail bed is Quincke's sign of aortic regurgitation. De Musset's is head nodding, Muller's is uvula pulsation and Corrigan's is a bounding carotid.

steps.x: Name an eponymous sign of AR.
AR, with **nail bed** pulsation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Quincke's sign.**

elim: Corrigan's is visible bounding carotid pulsation.
De Musset's is head nodding with each beat.
Muller's is pulsation of the uvula.
Traube's is a 'pistol shot' sound over the femoral artery.

steps.x: **D. Quincke's sign.** Nail bed = Quincke's.

practice.stem: A 32 year old man is 1.96 m tall with long fingers, a high-arched palate and lens dislocation. He has new exertional breathlessness. His pulse rate is 80 bpm, collapsing, and BP 150/50 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his aortic regurgitation?
practice.e: Marfan's syndrome causes aortic regurgitation through aortic root dilation. There is no fever to suggest endocarditis and no rheumatic history.

steps.x: The cause of AR: read the body habitus.
**Marfan's** features plus AR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Marfan's → **aortic root dilation** → AR.

elim: Bicuspid valves cause AS more than AR, without Marfanoid features.
Calcification is a disease of the elderly and causes AS.
No fever or embolic signs.
No history of rheumatic fever.

steps.x: **A. Aortic root dilation.** Marfan's + AR = root dilation.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has exertional chest pain and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 124/96 mmHg. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus rhythm with very tall R waves in V5-V6, deep S waves in V1-V2 and lateral T wave inversion.

practice.q: Which is the most likely ECG finding?
practice.e: Aortic stenosis causes LVH: tall lateral R waves, deep anterior S waves and lateral T inversion (strain). The echo then confirms the valve lesion.

steps.x: Interpret the ECG in suspected AS.

clues: ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids
steps.x: AS with tall voltages and lateral T inversion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **LVH with strain**.

elim: There is no ST elevation.
P waves conduct normally; sinus rhythm.
RVH gives a dominant R in V1 and right axis deviation.
No short PR or delta waves.

steps.x: **C. LVH with strain.** Pressure overload of the LV.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has a new murmur heard at a pre-operative assessment for a hip replacement. She reports breathlessness walking uphill. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 134/88 mmHg. There is an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Transthoracic echo is the gold standard for valve disease and grades the severity of AS before her operation.

steps.x: Diagnostic test for a suspected valve lesion.
Suspected, possibly symptomatic AS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transthoracic echo.**

elim: Catheterisation is invasive and reserved for pre-surgical coronary assessment.
CXR cannot grade the valve.
CT aortogram is for dissection or aneurysm.
Exercise testing is unsafe in symptomatic AS.

steps.x: **E. Transthoracic echocardiogram.**

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 64 mmHg. She is fit, independent and has a 'reasonable' life expectancy. She has had a gastrointestinal bleed on anticoagulation in the past. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/94 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Severe symptomatic AS needs valve replacement. A previous bleed on anticoagulation contraindicates a mechanical valve, and she is fit for open surgery, so a bioprosthetic valve.

steps.x: Management: choose the valve.
Needs AVR; fit for surgery; **cannot take lifelong warfarin**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bioprosthetic** AVR.

elim: Surveillance is for mild, asymptomatic AS.
Diuretics only relieve symptoms.
Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin.
TAVI is for frail, high-risk patients, typically over 80.

steps.x: **B. Bioprosthetic valve.** Anticoagulation contraindicated + fit for surgery.

practice.stem: An 87 year old man has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 70 mmHg. He has COPD, chronic kidney disease and is judged high risk for open-heart surgery. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 118/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: TAVI is for less fit, higher-risk patients, typically over 80. Monitoring is inappropriate for severe symptomatic AS.

steps.x: Management in a high-risk elderly patient.
Over 80, frail, high surgical risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TAVI.**

elim: Valvuloplasty is a short-term bridge only.
Open surgery is too high risk.
Mechanical valves are for younger patients.
Severe symptomatic AS needs intervention.

steps.x: **E. TAVI.** Frail, over 80, high risk.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man had a mechanical aortic valve replacement 3 days ago. He is recovering well with no bleeding. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. He asks which blood thinner he will need.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulation?
practice.e: Any mechanical heart valve needs lifelong warfarin (target INR 3.0 in the notes). DOACs are contraindicated, and aspirin alone is not enough.

steps.x: Long-term anticoagulation after valve replacement.
**Mechanical** valve.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lifelong **warfarin**.

elim: DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.
Aspirin alone does not prevent valve thrombosis.
Dabigatran increased thrombosis and bleeding with mechanical valves.
LMWH is a short-term bridge, not lifelong.

steps.x: **E. Warfarin.** Mechanical valve = warfarin, target INR 3.0.

practice.stem: A 77 year old man has severe aortic stenosis. Echocardiography shows a thick-walled left ventricle with a small cavity and normal ejection fraction. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 120/96 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the left ventricular changes?
practice.e: A fixed outflow obstruction raises afterload, so the LV thickens concentrically to maintain output. Volume overload (AR) causes eccentric hypertrophy and dilatation.

steps.x: Mechanism of the LV changes.

clues: thick-walled left ventricle with a small cavity
steps.x: Pressure overload pattern.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Concentric hypertrophy** against raised afterload.

elim: Volume overload dilates the LV, as in AR.
Eccentric hypertrophy is the AR pattern.
Infarction thins walls and reduces EF.
Sarcomere mutations cause HCM, not AS-driven LVH.

steps.x: **A. Concentric hypertrophy from increased afterload.** AS = pressure overload.

prompts.q: What are aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation, and what causes each?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age points to the cause of AS; rheumatic history or Marfan's to AR.

points.p: AS: valve narrows and obstructs LV outflow
AS causes: degenerative calcification (elderly), bicuspid valve (younger), rheumatic
AR: valve fails to close and blood leaks back into the LV
AR causes: rheumatic heart disease, aortic root dilation, endocarditis, Marfan's

prompts.q: Describe the symptoms and examination findings of aortic stenosis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: triad plus murmur, pulse, S2.

points.p: Triad: angina, syncope/presyncope, exertional dyspnoea
points.why: Exertional syncope is a red flag.

points.p: Ejection systolic murmur, right upper sternal edge (2nd ICS), radiates to carotids
points.why: Carotid radiation separates it from sclerosis.

points.p: Slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure (pulsus parvus et tardus)
Systolic thrill
Severe: soft or absent S2, S4, gradient over 40 mmHg

prompts.q: Describe the symptoms, murmur and signs of aortic regurgitation, including the eponyms.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: early diastolic + collapsing pulse + wide pulse pressure.

points.p: Breathlessness, fatigue, palpitations
Early diastolic, high-pitched, blowing murmur at the left sternal edge
Collapsing (water hammer) pulse and wide pulse pressure; soft S1
Quincke's (nail bed), Muller's (uvula), De Musset's (head nodding), Corrigan's (carotid)
points.why: Classic SBA distractors for each other.

prompts.q: How do you tell aortic stenosis from aortic sclerosis, and what is acute aortic regurgitation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: radiation and S2 decide sclerosis; acute AR = shock.

points.p: Sclerosis: ESM that does not radiate to the carotids
Sclerosis: normal S2, pulse character and volume
Acute AR: cardiogenic shock and acute heart failure
Acute AR most commonly from aortic dissection; Austin Flint murmur
points.why: Tearing pain with a new EDM.

prompts.q: Which investigations are used in aortic valve disease, and what does each show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: echo diagnoses; ECG shows LVH; CXR shows consequences.

points.p: Transthoracic echocardiogram is the gold standard
Echo gives the pressure gradient (AS) or degree of regurgitation (AR)
ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy in AS
CXR: cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema

prompts.q: Which echo and blood findings in severe AS trigger AVR referral, and what are the aortic root thresholds?

points.p: Vmax over 5 m/s
Valve area under 0.6 cm²
LVEF under 55%; BNP over 2x ULN; symptoms on exercise testing
Root under 4.5 cm yearly scan; 4.5-5.4 cm 3-monthly; over 5.5 cm or symptomatic: surgery

prompts.q: How is aortic stenosis managed, from mild to severe, including emergencies?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: symptoms or gradient over 40 mmHg = replace the valve.

points.p: Mild, asymptomatic: cardiology follow-up and monitoring
Diuretics (furosemide) for fluid overload
Severe or symptomatic (gradient over 40 mmHg): aortic valve replacement
Syncope with known AS is a red flag: urgent assessment

prompts.q: How do you choose between mechanical, bioprosthetic and TAVI, and what anticoagulation follows?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: young and fit = mechanical; frail over 80 = TAVI.

points.p: Mechanical: younger patients; lifelong warfarin, target INR 3.0
Mechanical contraindicated by age, life expectancy or anticoagulation contraindications
Bioprosthetic: older patients fit for open surgery
TAVI: less fit, higher risk, typically over 80
Coexisting carotid disease may need carotid endarterectomy

prompts.q: Why does aortic stenosis cause LVH, a slow-rising pulse and a soft S2?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fixed obstruction → pressure overload → concentric LVH.

points.p: Fixed obstruction to LV outflow raises afterload
Compensatory concentric LVH, later decompensation into heart failure
Narrowed orifice slows and reduces ejection: slow-rising pulse
Reduced valve closure sound: soft S2

prompts.q: Why does AR cause a wide pulse pressure and the Austin Flint murmur, and why do bicuspid valves stenose early?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: runoff, jet on the mitral leaflet, turbulence.

points.p: Diastolic backflow → volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy/dilation
Low diastolic pressure from rapid runoff: wide pulse pressure
Austin Flint: regurgitant jet impairs mitral valve opening, mimicking mitral stenosis
Bicuspid: turbulent flow accelerates fibrosis and calcification

glossary.Aortic stenosis: Narrowing of the aortic valve, obstructing blood leaving the left ventricle.
glossary.Aortic regurgitation: Leaking of the aortic valve so blood flows back into the left ventricle in diastole.
glossary.Aortic sclerosis: Thickening of the aortic valve without obstruction; ESM that does not radiate, normal S2 and pulse.
glossary.Bicuspid aortic valve: A congenital aortic valve with two leaflets instead of three, which stenoses decades early.
glossary.Degenerative calcification: Age-related calcium deposition stiffening the aortic valve; the commonest UK cause of AS.
glossary.Rheumatic heart disease: Valve scarring years after rheumatic fever; a common cause of AR worldwide.
glossary.Ejection systolic murmur: A crescendo-decrescendo murmur in systole, as in aortic stenosis.
glossary.Early diastolic murmur: A high-pitched blowing murmur starting just after S2, typical of aortic regurgitation.
glossary.Pulsus parvus et tardus: A small-volume, slow-rising pulse typical of severe aortic stenosis.
glossary.Slow-rising pulse: A pulse that takes longer than normal to reach its peak, typical of aortic stenosis.
glossary.Collapsing pulse: A pulse that rises fast then falls away abruptly; also called water hammer pulse, typical of AR.
glossary.Water hammer pulse: Another name for the collapsing pulse of aortic regurgitation.
glossary.Pulse pressure: Systolic minus diastolic blood pressure: narrow in AS, wide in AR.
glossary.Thrill: A palpable vibration over the heart from a loud murmur.
glossary.S2: The second heart sound, from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.
glossary.S4: An extra heart sound before S1 from the atrium pushing blood into a stiff ventricle.
glossary.Quincke's sign: Visible pulsation of the nail bed capillaries in aortic regurgitation.
glossary.Muller's sign: Pulsation of the uvula in aortic regurgitation.
glossary.De Musset's sign: Head nodding with each heartbeat in aortic regurgitation.
glossary.Corrigan's sign: Visible bounding pulsation of the carotid arteries in aortic regurgitation.
glossary.Austin Flint murmur: A mid-diastolic apical rumble in severe AR, from the jet stopping the mitral valve opening.
glossary.Aortic dissection: A tear in the aortic wall lining; the commonest cause of acute aortic regurgitation.
glossary.Aortic root dilation: Widening of the first part of the aorta, which stretches the valve and causes regurgitation.
glossary.Marfan's syndrome: Inherited connective tissue disorder causing tall stature, lens dislocation and aortic root dilation.
glossary.LVH: Left ventricular hypertrophy: thickening of the left ventricle wall.
glossary.Concentric hypertrophy: Even thickening of the ventricular wall with a small cavity, from pressure overload.
glossary.Eccentric hypertrophy: Ventricular dilation with wall growth, from volume overload.
glossary.Afterload: The pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.
glossary.Transthoracic echocardiogram: Ultrasound of the heart through the chest wall; the gold standard for valve disease.
glossary.Peak gradient: The maximum pressure difference across the valve on echo; above 40 mmHg is severe AS.
glossary.Vmax: Peak velocity of blood through the aortic valve on echo.
glossary.Valve area: The opening area of the aortic valve; normal is 3-4 cm².
glossary.LVEF: Left ventricular ejection fraction: the percentage of blood pumped out with each beat.
glossary.NT-proBNP: A blood marker released by stretched ventricles; raised in heart failure.
glossary.TAVI: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a new valve placed via a catheter, usually from the femoral artery.
glossary.Mechanical valve: A durable artificial valve that needs lifelong warfarin.
glossary.Bioprosthetic valve: A tissue (animal) valve that does not need lifelong warfarin but wears out.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio: a measure of warfarin effect.
glossary.Warfarin: A vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant; the only oral anticoagulant for mechanical valves.
glossary.DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban; contraindicated with mechanical valves.
glossary.Furosemide: A loop diuretic that removes excess fluid.
glossary.Carotid endarterectomy: Surgery to remove plaque from the carotid artery to reduce stroke risk.
